qt: to the Commission Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

On 14 July 2026, the EU held accession conferences with Montenegro and Albania. For Montenegro, the parties provisionally closed negotiations on competition and customs union, meaning that, in total, 18 out of 33 negotiating chapters have been provisionally closed. As regards Albania, the parties provisionally closed negotiating chapters on science and research, education and culture, and external relations. Albania has now opened all negotiating chapters and provisionally closed three of them1. Against this background: 1.

Given the varying degrees of reform progress between the two countries, how does the Commission ensure that the opening of thematic clusters and the provisional closure of chapters are based exclusively on merit and full compliance with the Copenhagen criteria, particularly regarding the rule of law and the fight against corruption and organised crime?
Does the Commission consider that the current accelerated pace of negotiation risks lowering accession standards?
Will the Commission commit to recommending the reopening of closed chapters if it is shown that the candidate countries have not achieved adequate progress in their respective accession chapters?
The Council, ‘EU enlargement advances with four accession conferences in one day’, 14 July 2026, https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/news/20260714-four-accession-conferences-in-one-day/. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.11.2026) The 2020 revised Enlargement Methodology1 made the accession process more predictable, credible, dynamic, and subject to stronger political steering, placing the Fundamentals and the rule of law at the centre of the process. Progress under this cluster determines the overall pace of negotiations. No chapter may be provisionally closed before a candidate country has met the interim benchmarks on the Fundamentals cluster. In cases of serious or prolonged stagnation or backsliding, provisionally closed chapters may also be reopened. Any such step should be informed by the assessment from the Commission in its enlargement package, which also looks at the overall compliance with the Copenhagen criteria, including the rule of law, and it would remain with the Member States to decide. The accession process therefore remains demanding and merit based. In the case of the Western Balkans, regional cooperation and good neighbourly relations are essential aspects of the accession process, as set out in the Stabilisation and Association Process. Alignment with the Common Foreign and Security Policy of the EU is a key signal of shared values and strategic orientation in the current geopolitical context. Future enlargements will also rely on stronger safeguards, with a new generation of accession treaties being designed to reduce the risk of post-accession backsliding. Enlargement will continue to advance based on the pace of reforms in candidate countries, while taking into account the EU’s capacity to integrate new members effectively.
